beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the ask lands answered
beats.narration: Hi, I am Kehinde Obidele and this video is about how much information a Yoruba accent mark actually carries. I grew up speaking Yoruba, and most Yoruba text online has the marks stripped off it. I built a small model to put them back, but before I trained anything I wanted to know what the marks were even worth.
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Kehinde Obidele and this video is about how much information a Yoruba accent mark actually carries. I grew up speaking Yoruba, and most Yoruba text online has the marks stripped off it. I built a small model to put them back, but before I trained anything I wanted to know what the marks were even worth.

show.event: Cream page, spark, serif greeting 'Hi, Kehinde' above the composer
The ask types itself in, character by character
Send button arms terracotta, running indicator reads 'measuring the marks…'

props.command: Yoruba writing uses dots and tone marks that most keyboards drop, so "oko" could be oko (farm), ọkọ (husband) or ọkọ̀ (vehicle). Before I train a model to put the marks back, help me ask the right question: how many BITS of information do those marks actually carry, how much of that can be settled by the word alone, and how much can only be settled by the sentence around it?
output: 1.64 bits per character, knowing the letter
0.61 bits per word left, knowing the word
the rest is what the sentence has to supply

beats.new_visual_element: Hesitant writer, the overview corrected on screen
beats.narration: I used to think of the marks as decoration you could drop. They are not. They carry information you can measure in bits, and whatever is left over is the only thing a model is actually for.
beats.narration_text: I used to think of the marks as decoration you could drop. They are not. They carry information you can measure in bits, and whatever is left over is the only thing a model is actually for.

beats.new_visual_element: One spelling fans out to three words (Kehinde's Manim, segment 1)
beats.narration: Type oko with no marks and you have merged three different words into one. Farm. Husband. Vehicle. Same three letters, and the keyboard quietly drops the difference. Most Yoruba text online lives in exactly that collapsed state.

All three hold together under the single unmarked spelling

beats.new_visual_element: Per-letter entropy of the marks (Kehinde's Manim, segment 2)
beats.narration: So I measured it first. Knowing only the base letter, guessing its mark costs one point six four bits. Look at the shape. E and O are the expensive ones.
beats.narration_text: So I measured it first. Knowing only the base letter, guessing its mark costs one point six four bits. Look at the shape. E and O are the expensive ones.

shot.media_note: Segment 2 of the same animation: the Shannon entropy formula and the per-letter bar chart, measured on 2.0M restorable characters of his training corpus.

show.event: Title sets: 'Guessing the mark from the base letter alone'
The entropy formula draws in: H = -sum p(c) log2 p(c)
Eight bars grow to their measured heights, gold for the tall pair
e 2.56 and o 2.54 stand clear above a 1.57, i 1.55, u 1.46
The tail lands: s 0.99, n 0.53, m 0.01

beats.new_visual_element: Letter, word, sentence: the information ladder (Kehinde's Manim, segment 3)
beats.narration: Now give it the whole word. The cost drops to nought point six one bits. That is the residue, the part the word cannot settle. Only the sentence can. And that gap is why this needs a model at all.
beats.narration_text: Now give it the whole word. The cost drops to nought point six one bits. That is the residue, the part the word cannot settle. Only the sentence can. And that gap is why this needs a model at all.

shot.media_note: Segment 3: the three-rung ladder that closes the animation on the thesis.

show.event: Rung one sets: 'knowing the letter', 1.64 bits per character in gold
Rung two: 'knowing the word', 0.61 bits per word left
Rung three: 'knowing the sentence', and the answer reads 'the model's job' in teal
All three rungs hold together, the residue visibly shrinking down the ladder

beats.narration: And the shape of that chart is not an accident. It falls straight out of the orthography. In my mark scheme, E and O are the only letters that can take a dot and a tone. S takes a dot and no tone at all. So E and O carry the most uncertainty because they have the most legal options.

props.title: ami/marks.py
props.code:
CLASSES = ["NONE", "GRAVE", "ACUTE", "DOT", "DOT_GRAVE", "DOT_ACUTE"]

# Which classes each base letter may take. Yoruba specific:
# only e, o (and s) dot; s takes no tone.
ALLOWED = {
    "a": {"NONE", "GRAVE", "ACUTE"},
    "e": {"NONE", "GRAVE", "ACUTE", "DOT", "DOT_GRAVE", "DOT_ACUTE"},
    "i": {"NONE", "GRAVE", "ACUTE"},
    "o": {"NONE", "GRAVE", "ACUTE", "DOT", "DOT_GRAVE", "DOT_ACUTE"},
    "u": {"NONE", "GRAVE", "ACUTE"},
    "s": {"NONE", "DOT"},
}
props.sparkLine: Six legal options, not an open vocabulary.

beats.new_visual_element: Three systems on the same held-out test set
beats.narration: Here is what that buys. Leave the text unmarked and you are at thirty-nine percent character accuracy. A lookup table that always picks the most frequent form gets seventy-seven. The model that reads the sentence gets ninety-two point four.

beats.new_visual_element: Criteria card, what it handles and where it slips
beats.narration: Now where it fails, because that matters more. It is trained on published prose, so informal Yoruba and heavy code switching are weaker. Names are the worst case, a name it has never seen just gets the most probable marking. And tone confusions are most of what is left. It has learned the alphabet. The music is harder.

beats.new_visual_element: Verdict artifact, what the bits bought
beats.narration: So here is the thing I would take from this. Measure the problem before you model it. The bits told me a lookup table would get most of the way and then stall, and they told me exactly how much was left for context to do. One point two nine million parameters was enough, on a laptop CPU.

artifactLines: The marks are information, and information is measurable.
About 1.64 bits from the letter, 0.61 left once you know the word.

beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the viewer's prompt typed
beats.narration: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take a writing system you know that uses marks, accents, tones, vowel points, anything, and work out how much information those marks actually carry. How many forms can each base letter legally take? Which words are ambiguous without context? Then tell me whether a lookup table would be enough, or whether it really needs a model. Do not guess, count. That last line is the point. Most of the time you can tell whether a problem needs machine learning before you write any.

props.segment: Measure it before you model it
props.command: Take a writing system that uses marks: accents, tones, vowel points, anything. Work out how much information those marks carry. How many forms can each base letter legally take? Which words are ambiguous once the marks come off? Then tell me whether a frequency lookup table would be enough, or whether the remaining ambiguity genuinely needs a model. Do not guess. Count.
